headline: Hawaii's Seabirds Find Refuge Behind Fortress Fence
meta_description: A $1.7 million predator exclusion fence on Kauai now protects thousands of endangered seabirds and Hawaiian bats from invasive predators.
summary_short: Completed in 2022, a high-tech predator fence encircling 168 acres on Kauai's Kīlauea Point is already helping endangered seabirds raise chicks safely for the first time…
body:
Four years after its completion in 2022, an 11,200-foot-long predator exclusion fence on Kauai has transformed 168 acres of Hawaiian shoreline into a sanctuary where endangered seabirds are now thriving. The fence, which cost $1.7 million to build, encircles critical nesting habitat at Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge and has already allowed species like the Hawaiian petrel, Newell's shearwater, and red-footed boobies to raise their chicks in safety. Where these birds once faced constant threats from feral cats and pigs, they now follow their ancestral instincts undisturbed, nesting at sites that would have been deadly traps just five years earlier.

The fence itself is an engineering marvel, originally developed in New Zealand to combat the Pacific's most destructive invasive mammals. Its design is uncompromising: too high for cats or foxes to leap, topped with a claw-proof hood, buried deep enough to prevent pigs from burrowing beneath, and fitted with metal mesh fine enough to block rats yet strong enough to resist any animal's teeth. The protected terrain at Nihokū and Mokolea Point offers additional advantages—minimal artificial light to disorient birds that navigate by stars and moon, and no powerlines or elevated structures to cause collisions.

The results speak for themselves. A similar fence on Oahu quadrupled the number of Newell's shearwater chicks within its first several years. Beyond seabirds, the Kauai fence also shelters the Critically Endangered Hawaiian hoary bat and nēnē, Hawaii's state bird. Until the island can adequately manage or remove invasive predators more broadly, this specialized barrier will remain essential—a lifeline ensuring that Hawaii's iconic aviators survive for generations to come.
quick_facts: 168 acres of seabird nesting habitat protected
$1.7 million cost to build and install
Protects endangered Hawaiian petrels and Newell's shearwater
Designed to block cats, foxes, pigs, and rats
